routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Return deduplicated changes keyed by id.

Equality covers id, component, units and the set of dependencies. The same id
with any difference is a conflicting definition and fails, because silently
keeping the first or the last would make plans depend on input order.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Return the caller-supplied release journal as a set of change IDs.

This is replay state, not authority: the caller owns the persisted journal and
this service only reads it, so an unknown ID cannot be silently dropped — it
would make "already applied" mean something the caller never recorded. The
unknown-ID check itself belongs to planner, which owns the graph keys.

comments: # depends_on defaults to an empty list. A non-list (including None or a bare
# string) is malformed input, not an empty set, so it must fail explicitly
# rather than silently weakening the graph.
# Each entry is checked as a string before being put into a set: an unhashable
# entry (list/object) would otherwise raise TypeError and break the JSON result.
# Same hazard as dependencies: validate entries as nonempty strings before the
# set() call so an unhashable journal entry becomes invalid-change, not a crash.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

This module owns input validation, change identity and replay state. It never
looks at policy or ordering: planner calls it first and receives normalized data
so graph construction can assume every record has an id, component, positive
units and a set of string dependencies.

Why here: a malformed request must be rejected before any graph or budget work
runs, otherwise a later error could look like a domain failure. Keeping
normalization in one place is also what makes the dedup comparison exact
(id/component/units/dependency set) for both the plan and rollback paths.

routines.name: _topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of all changes.

Ties among currently eligible changes are broken lexicographically by id and
the graph is untouched while ordering, so the same request always yields the
same actions. Any change not emitted by the walk is part of a cycle.

comments: # A dependency naming an id absent from the request cannot be ordered;
# it is rejected before ordering so the error is not reported as a cycle.
# Rollback undoes what the caller's journal says is deployed, in the reverse
# of the full order. The budget was validated above but is deliberately not
# a cap: undoing past a limit is the recovery path, and blocking it would
# leave the environment stuck.
# Budget applies to emitted units only, after dedup and replay: applied changes
# already consumed whatever they consumed and are not charged again.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

policy first (environment/action/budget legality), journal next (normalization,

routines.name: limit_for

Errors are raised in a fixed order (environment, action, budget) so an input
with several problems reports one stable code instead of varying by key order.

routines.name: _retention_closure
routines.docstring:
Return the applied IDs that rollback must keep because `retained` needs them.

The walk follows the *full* dependency graph in `changes`, not the applied
subset: a retained change depends on definitions from the request, and an
applied change reachable through an unapplied one is still required by the
retained change, so truncating at unapplied nodes would roll back something
retention asked to keep. Only applied IDs are collected — an unapplied
dependency is not part of the journal and rollback never emits it anyway. The
graph is already known to be acyclic here, but a seen-set keeps the walk linear and
would also stop a repeat visit rather than recurse forever.

# checks but before any action list exists, so a bad retain list rejects the

# blocking it would leave the environment stuck.

routines.docstring:
Return normalized, de-duplicated changes in first-seen order.

Each entry: {"id", "component", "units", "depends_on" (tuple, sorted, set)}.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring: Validate the caller-supplied release journal and return it as a set.

routines.name: deduplicate
routines.docstring:
Collapse identical records; a conflicting duplicate id is a hard error.

Identity covers id, component, units and the set of dependencies. We never
pick a "winner" between conflicting rows: the choice would change both the
billed units and the execution order, so the caller must resolve it.

routines.name: replay
routines.docstring:
De-duplicate changes, then reconcile the persisted journal against them.

Returns (unique_changes, applied_ids, total_units). `total_units` is the
sum over the de-duplicated changes and is what budget checks are compared
against; already-applied entries contribute to it but are removed from the
emitted set by the planner, so they never consume new budget.

comments: # Nonempty str only. `True`/`1`/["a"] are never valid identifiers, and a
# bare string is *not* accepted as a dependency list: "a,b" must not be
# read as ["a", "b"].
# `type(...) is int` excludes bool, because bool is an int subclass and
# `units: true` would otherwise be billed as one unit.
# Sorting + set makes duplicate comments/ordering irrelevant to
# both identity and the graph, so an identical record repeated in
# a different but equivalent shape still collapses (SPEC G1).
# else: identical duplicate, already accounted for once.
# An applied id that no longer exists means the journal and the manifest
# have drifted apart; the safe answer is to refuse, not to guess.
# Every dependency edge must point at a change in this request as well;
# otherwise ordering it is undefined.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Journal owns everything about *which changes exist and which are already out*:
field validation, duplicate identity, the persisted release journal (`applied`)
and replay accounting (units). It deliberately knows nothing about graph order;
it only hands the normalized changes to the planner (see ARCHITECTURE.md §2).

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Kahn's algorithm, always taking the lexicographically smallest eligible id.

SPEC requires tie-breaking "among currently eligible changes", i.e. nodes
whose dependencies are all already emitted -- not simply sorting the final
list by id. Example: b -> a, and c independent. Eligible set starts {b, c};
take b, then {a, c}; take a, then c, giving [b, a, c]. A plain sort would
give [a, b, c], which emits a before its dependency.

Cycles are detected globally (indegree > 0 after the loop), including
cycles entirely inside the already-applied subgraph. A graph the caller
describes inconsistently is rejected as a whole rather than partially
ordered: emitting "the acyclic part" would be a plausible-looking,
unsafe answer.

routines.name: _emit
routines.docstring: Return the ids in `order` that belong to `keep`, preserving that order.

comments: # The only failure constructor: every rejection path funnels through it, so
# no branch can leak partial actions or a nonzero unit count.
# Self-dependency is just another edge: indegree never reaches zero
# and it surfaces as dependency-cycle below.
# Policy first (environment/action/budget), then the journal. This order
# is part of the contract when several problems coexist.
# `applied` defaults to [] but a non-list value is a journal error, not
# silently treated as empty.
# Reverse of the *full* deterministic order, keeping only applied rows:
# dependents are always undone before the things they depend on, which
# is what makes the persisted state roll back in a safe sequence.
# SPEC: rollback validates the budget field but does not cap it.
# plan: unapplied changes only. Already-applied entries still satisfied
# their dependents' edges above but cost no new budget.
# Budget is checked after replay/de-duplication and after dropping applied
# rows. Over-budget is all-or-nothing: never trim to "the first actions
# that fit", because such a prefix could be executed as a half release.
planner.py.moduleNote: Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the requested budget; raises PolicyError on a policy violation.

Policy runs before journal parsing on purpose: the documented order is
environment/action first, then change records (ARCHITECTURE.md section 4).

comments: # G1: both environments support both actions. Anything outside this matrix is
# rejected before any graph work, so an unsupported action can never emit
# partial actions. If a later goal restricts rollback to staging, this is the
# single place to change (see ARCHITECTURE.md, section "实施顺序与回退顺序").

# `in frozenset` attempt an unhashable lookup and raise TypeError out of

# Covers missing, null, non-string and unknown actions alike.
# `type(x) is not int` rather than isinstance: bool is a subclass of int, so
# `True` would otherwise pass as budget 1 and silently skew accounting.
# Non-negative integers only; floats, numeric strings and null all fail.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate a rollback `retain` list and return it as a set.

CHANGE-G2.md item 3: `retain` lists ids that are already applied and must
stay out of the rollback ("must remain"). Two rejection cases, one code:

* malformed -- the value is not a list, or any element is not a nonempty
  str (bools, ints, nested lists all fail for the same reason ids fail
  elsewhere: an id is a nonempty string, nothing else);
* non-applied -- an id that the caller asks to retain is not in the
  persisted journal. Retaining something that was never applied is not
  harmlessly redundant: it means the caller's idea of the release state
  disagrees with the journal, and silently ignoring it would roll back a
  change the caller believes is protected.

`records` is the raw field value; a missing field must be passed as []
(the caller's default), because an explicit `null` is malformed, not empty.
The transitive "also keep its applied dependencies" expansion is a graph
question and therefore lives in the planner, not here.

routines.name: protected_by_retain
routines.docstring:
Ids that a rollback must keep: `retained` plus its applied dependencies.

CHANGE-G2.md item 3 says to keep "the transitive dependencies that are
applied and required by those retained changes". Walking the dependency
edges transitively (not just one level) is what keeps the graph consistent:
removing a dependency of a change that stays applied would leave a live
change whose prerequisite is gone.

This is deliberately a *pure graph closure*: it does not consult `applied`.
A dependency of a retained change is part of the closure even if it was
never applied; the caller intersects the closure with the applied set when
emitting, so the "and applied" clause of the spec is applied exactly once,
in one place.

Unknown dependency targets cannot appear here: journal.replay rejects them
with `unknown-dependency` before the graph is ever built.

routines.name: _emit
routines.docstring: Return the ids in `order` that belong to `keep`, preserving that order.

# would push the same id twice; cycles are already excluded by the

comments: # G2: this release is staging-only. `production` is still a *recognised*
# environment (it must not degrade into `invalid-environment`, which would tell

# rejected by the `production-frozen` gate below before anything else is

# Only staging may proceed, and it supports both actions.
# CHANGE-G2.md item 2: a staging plan's budget is capped by policy, not by the
# request. The cap is a hard ceiling -- a request asking for more does not
# raise it, it lowers the effective budget back to the cap.

# requires `production-frozen` even when the graph is malformed. Ordering

# Rollback keeps the G1 rule that the budget field is validated but never
# caps the operation, so its effective budget is the request unchanged

policy must be able to reject a request without touching the graph at all

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and collapse identical duplicates.

Equality covers id, component, units and the *set* of dependencies.
Replay happens here, before accounting and before graph construction:
counting duplicates would double the budget and duplicate edges would
create phantom cycles.  The first surviving record is kept; ordering is
decided later from the id, so the input order does not leak into the plan.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring: Validate the caller-supplied persisted release journal.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the rollback retention list.

In contrast to `applied`, an absent `retain` key means "retain nothing"
(the caller passes [] in that case).  An explicit null, a non-array or a
non-string entry is malformed.  Entries must be *already applied* changes:
retaining something that was never applied has no meaning, and retaining
an id that is not even in the graph is equally invalid (the retain list is
not a graph edge, so it does not count as an unknown dependency).

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return every change id in one deterministic dependency order.

The order is computed over the FULL deduplicated graph: `plan` emits a
subsequence of it and `rollback` replays its reverse, so a change keeps
its position no matter which subset is applied or retained.

Tie-breaking: each step emits the lexicographically smallest change whose
dependencies have all been emitted already, re-evaluating immediately
after every single emission (Kahn with a sorted eligible set).  Re-checking
per node (not per round) is required for the rollback contract: a change
freed by an emission must be emitted before an unrelated larger id, so a
plan can be rolled back by simply reversing it.  For graphs without
dependencies this is exactly the old "plan is sorted by id" behaviour.

routines.name: dependency_closure
routines.docstring:
Return seeds plus all of their transitive dependencies.

Never includes dependents, so retaining X only protects X and what it
needs.  A single forward pass over the topological order suffices: each
dependency appears before the retained change that needs it.

comments: # All error codes this module reports.  They are raised as JournalError and
# funneled into the exact failure object by planner.failure().
# bool is not a str subclass so this is enough; an empty id/component is
# rejected because it cannot name a change in the journal.
# `type(...) is int` (not isinstance) is deliberate: JSON `true`/`false`
# parse to bool, which is an int subclass.  Booleans are not integers.
# `depends_on` defaults to [] when the key is absent, but an explicit null
# or any non-array is malformed and must fail as invalid-change rather
# than being silently treated as "no dependencies".
# Same id, different identity: the journal cannot say which
# revision is live, so refuse rather than guess.  Dependency sets
# compared as sets, so ["a", "b"] and ["b", "a", "a"] are equal.
# Deliberately NO default for an absent key: SPEC says the journal is
# supplied by the caller, and neither an explicit null nor a missing list
# may be read as "nothing applied" (that would turn a malformed rollback
# into a silent no-op).  Only a real array is accepted.
# Dependencies are deduplicated so duplicate edges (e.g. depends_on:
# ["a", "a"]) count once and cannot fake a cycle.
# Keep `eligible` sorted by id: a freed id may be smaller than
# the ones already waiting.
# A waiting node's dependencies were all verified to exist, so a node
# still waiting belongs to a cycle.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Owns everything that turns caller-supplied JSON into trustworthy release
data: change validation, replay (dedup/conflict) identity, the persisted
``applied`` journal, the rollback ``retain`` list, and the deterministic
topological order.  No imports from other project modules (dependency
direction is release -> planner -> {policy, journal}).

comments: # Normalization and replay run before the graph: duplicates would
# otherwise inflate the units total and add parallel edges that can
# look like a cycle.
# `applied` is required for BOTH actions.  The journal is the caller's
# persisted state, and a missing key must not be read as "nothing
# applied": for rollback that would emit nothing and for plan it would
# re-plan work that may already be live.  A missing key is malformed
# (invalid-change) exactly like an explicit null.  `retain` is the one
# documented default (empty) and only exists for rollback.
# `retain` is a rollback-only field; for plan it is ignored entirely.
# `applied` must name known changes; otherwise replay cannot be trusted.
# This is a membership error even though the code is unknown-dependency,
# because the journal is the caller's claim about this same graph.
# "Retain the transitive dependencies that are APPLIED and required by
# the retained changes": only applied nodes join the keep-set, so an
# unapplied intermediate dependency is not itself kept.  retain
# membership was already validated by read_retain (invalid-retain).
# Reverse of the FULL deterministic order (not of the applied subset),
# minus the retained changes and their applied dependencies.
# The budget field does not cap rollback, even though `budget` was
# validated; units still report the units actually emitted.
# plan: only unapplied changes, in the same deterministic order.  Applied
# entries satisfy their dependencies and consume no new budget, but a
# dependency that is neither applied nor unapplied was already rejected by
# topological_order (unknown-dependency).
# Budget accounting happens AFTER dedup and replay: `units` counts only
# what would really be executed, so duplicate records or already-applied
# entries cannot exhaust the quota.  For staging the policy already capped
# the effective budget, so a request above the quota fails here too.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Return deduplicated changes in first-seen order.

Each change is a dict with ``id``, ``component``, ``units`` and a sorted
``dependencies`` tuple. Identical duplicates collapse; conflicting ones fail.

routines.docstring: Return the persisted release journal as a set of change IDs.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Return the retained change IDs as a set; ``retain`` defaults to empty.

Entries are only checked for type here. Whether each retained ID is known
and already applied is decided after the graph is built.

routines.name: build_graph
routines.docstring: Index changes by ID and validate graph targets and the applied journal.

Normalize a validated request into its change list, applied set and graph.

``retain`` is read for rollback only, where the journal must confirm each
retained ID is a known, already applied change.
